 Energy Crude oil prices fall below $90 a barrel as Vance blames GOP election defeat on Iran war
 Published Wed, Nov 4 2026 11:43 AM EST Updated 11 Min Ago Spencer Kimball @spencekimball WATCH LIVE In this article
 @LCO27J 
 @LCO27F 
 Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:56 02:56 Vice President Vance blames Iran war for Republican midterm losses Squawk on the Street Crude oil prices tumbled on Wednesday after Vice President JD Vance blamed the war against Iran for Republican midterm election reversals. 
 U.S. West Texas Intermediate was 7% lower at $89.40. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, were down nearly 8% to $95.41.
 "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in a social media post Wednesday. "The president himself said so last night."
 Democrats swept the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections, giving the party leverage to pressure President Donald Trump to end the unpopular war that has spiked gasoline and diesel prices. Traders appear to be betting that the election defeat will push Trump to negotiate with Iran. 
 Vance said a lot of voters who supported Trump in 2024 appear to have abandoned the GOP last night due to their dissatisfication with the war. 
Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that he has no immediate plans to strike Iran. The oil market had priced in the risk of a major escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
 The oil market is in a "shoot first, ask questions" later mode as emotions run high after the unexpected election results, said Rebecca Babin senior energy trader at CIBC. 
 Many observers expected a Democrat tsunami could push Trump to escalate with Iran, Babin said. But "Vance's commentary and the public lack of backing from key allies have challenged that assumption," she said. 
 Oil futures have sold off more than 14% this week as senior U.S. and Iranian officials indicated they're open to a diplomatic settlement to the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
 "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. 
 "But everyone knows why we lost," the vice president said. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
 -- CNBC's Pippa Stevens contributed to this report.
